summary: Revises RIPv2 cryptographic authentication, adding details of using the SHA family of hash algorithms, where RFC 2082 specified only MD5. It obsoletes RFC 2082 and updates RFC 2453.

plainLanguage.summary: Routers using RIP sign their messages so others know who sent them. This update says how to sign using newer, stronger signature methods than the old one.

questions: how does ripv2 key rollover work
subtitle: How RIPv2 routers sign their messages with a keyed hash, now with the SHA family as well as MD5.

tldr.problem: RIPv2 originally offered no authentication or a cleartext password, both open to passive attacks, and the cryptographic option from RFC 2082 only used Keyed-MD5.
tldr.mechanism: RIPv2 messages carry an authentication trailer holding a keyed hash. The hash is Keyed-MD5 or HMAC with SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512, chosen per key, and keys are identified by a Key ID and rolled over in overlapping lifetimes.
tldr.outcome: This document obsoletes RFC 2082 and updates RFC 2453. It guards against forgery and modification but gives no confidentiality, and the authors say it is not the final word on RIPv2 authentication.

today: RFC 4822 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2082 and updates RFC 2453. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why RIPv2 Needed Better Authentication
sections.content:
RIPv2 offers unauthenticated service, as classical RIP does, or a cleartext password. Both are vulnerable to passive attacks: anyone who captures traffic on the wire can read the password and use it to inject false information into the routing system.

The original cryptographic scheme, RFC 2082, used Keyed-MD5. This document keeps that algorithm but adds the SHA family of hash algorithms and the HMAC technique. The RFC gives three reasons: reports that created concern about MD5's ultimate strength, users such as several governments that require SHA for policy reasons, and the belief that HMAC is a stronger construction than the one used originally.

Because the original mechanism was algorithm-independent and widely deployed, backward compatibility was kept, which limited the change to adding a new family of algorithms. The mechanism does not provide confidentiality: messages stay in the clear, which the RFC considers acceptable because a routing protocol exists to advertise topology.
sections.plainLanguage: A plain password written on a postcard can be read and copied by anyone. A secret stamp that changes with each message is much harder to fake, so routers use that instead.

sections.title: The Authenticated RIPv2 Packet
sections.content:
The normal RIPv2 header and route entries are unchanged. What changes is the first 20-octet entry, whose 16-octet password field is reused. The Authentication Type is 3, meaning Cryptographic Hash Function, and the entry carries the packet length, a Key ID, the Authentication Data Length and a sequence number.

  • RIPv2 Packet Length: 16 bits, the offset to the end of the regular RIPv2 packet, not counting the authentication trailer.
  • Key ID: 8 bits. Combined with the network interface it identifies the Security Association in use.
  • Authentication Data Length: 8 bits, the length of the trailing authentication data. It makes the scheme independent of the algorithm.
  • Sequence Number: 32 bits, and it MUST be non-decreasing for all messages from a given source router with a given Key ID.

The keyed hash output is carried in a trailer after the regular packet, and the figure shows it as 20 bytes with HMAC-SHA1.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message gets a little label on the front that says which secret key was used and a counter number, and a signature stuck on the back.

sections.title: RIPv2 Security Associations
sections.content:
The RFC calls the RIPv2 Security Association central to the specification. It is the set of shared parameters a legitimate sender or receiver needs, and it is always tied to an interface rather than to a router. An implementation MUST support at least 2 concurrent Security Associations on each RIP interface, because key rollover is mandatory.

The minimum contents are a Key ID, the authentication algorithm, the authentication key, a sequence number, a start time and a stop time. The algorithm is never sent on the wire. The possible values are KEYED-MD5, HMAC-SHA-1, HMAC-SHA-256, HMAC-SHA-384 and HMAC-SHA-512. The key MUST NOT ever be sent in cleartext over any protocol.

The sender picks any valid association for the outgoing interface. The receiver uses the interface and the Key ID to find the right one. Setting the stop time to never expire is permitted but not recommended, since it reduces security compared with periodic rekeying.
sections.plainLanguage: A security association is like a secret-club card: it says which key you share, which kind of signature to use and when the card works.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Messages
sections.content:
When sending, the router builds the packet as usual, picks an association by outbound interface, fills in the Key ID and data length, runs the algorithm-specific computation and writes the result into the Authentication Data field. The UDP checksum SHOULD be calculated but MAY be set to zero, since the cryptographic check gives stronger integrity protection.

When receiving, the router looks up the association from the Key ID and interface. With no valid association, it stops processing and SHOULD log a security event. Otherwise it computes the authentication data and compares it with the received value. A mismatch means the message MUST be discarded and SHOULD be logged.

The sequence number is checked next. If the neighbor has been heard from recently enough to have viable routes and the number is lower than the last one received, the message MUST be discarded. After connectivity to a neighbor is lost, the receiver SHOULD accept a sequence number of zero or a higher one. A router that has forgotten its sequence number but remembers its association MUST send its first packet with sequence number zero, which leaves a small opening for replay. Implementers SHOULD therefore use non-volatile storage.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver checks the signature, and also checks the counter only goes up. A message with a wrong signature or an old counter gets thrown away.

sections.title: Keyed-MD5 and HMAC-SHA Processing
sections.content:
With Keyed-MD5 the authentication key is always 16 octets. It is appended to the packet in memory, followed by the MD5 padding and message length fields, and the digest is computed as defined in RFC 1321.

With the HMAC algorithms, the document uses the FIPS 198 terminology. The key is prepared to be exactly L octets, where L is the hash length (for example 20 with SHA-1). A longer key is hashed and a shorter key is padded with zeros. The Authentication Data field is first filled with a constant called Apad. The inner hash is H(Ko XOR Ipad || packet) and the outer hash is H(Ko XOR Opad || First-Hash).

The output is NOT truncated, so the Authentication Data Length equals the digest size of the hash. Hash functions with larger output sizes therefore make packets larger on the wire. Keys known to be weak MUST NOT be used.
sections.plainLanguage: The router mixes the secret key into the message twice and squishes it into a short fingerprint. Anyone without the key cannot make the same fingerprint.

sections.title: Key Management and Rollover
sections.content:
Implementations MUST support storing more than one key at a time, tied to a lifetime and a Key ID, and MUST support manual key distribution, such as an operator typing in the key on a router console. Manual deletion of active associations MUST also be supported. Operators are strongly encouraged to rekey regularly, with a lifetime such as 24 hours.

Smooth rollover works because the Key ID and interface select the key. The receiver MUST NOT try all configured keys, since that creates an easily exploited denial-of-service attack. To roll over, each system gets the new association several minutes before the old one expires and before the new lifetime begins, so for a while either key authenticates.

The RFC deliberately left out an integrated key management protocol. Such protocols have a history of subtle flaws, and including one would risk having to change every RIPv2 implementation. The Key ID field is meant as a hook for a future standard protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers can hold two keys at once, like having an old and a new house key, so changing locks does not leave anyone stuck outside.

sections.title: Conformance Requirements
sections.content:
Every conforming implementation MUST implement Keyed-MD5 and HMAC-SHA1. It SHOULD also implement HMAC-SHA-256, HMAC-SHA-384 and HMAC-SHA-512. Extra algorithms are allowed if they are publicly and openly specified.

Implementations MUST support manual key distribution, smooth key rollover and at least 2 concurrent associations. The user documentation ought to explain how to configure smooth rollover, and implementations SHOULD support a standard key management protocol once the IETF standardizes one. The RFC states that its Security Considerations section is an integral part of the specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Every router must know the old and one newer way to sign, and should know the even stronger ones too.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The mechanism is believed secure against passive attacks, but protection against active attacks is incomplete. The main gap is a recently rebooted router that lacks non-volatile storage for its associations and last sequence numbers.

Two pathological cases MUST be handled. During rollover, routers SHOULD detect which associations neighbors use and send with both old and new until all neighbors have switched or the old one expires. If the last association on an interface expires, the router MUST notify the network manager and SHOULD treat that association as having an infinite lifetime, rather than fall back to no authentication. Any expiration MUST be logged, and implementations SHOULD offer a fail secure option.

Using SNMP to configure associations or the authentication type is NOT RECOMMENDED, because a compromise there could cascade to all routers. Confidentiality and traffic analysis protection are not provided. Key entry in hexadecimal SHOULD be supported, since text-only entry makes many key bits predictable. The IESG note says it approved the document to encourage rapid migration away from Keyed-MD5, and urged automated key management work.
sections.plainLanguage: The signatures stop outsiders from faking messages, but a router that forgets its counter after a restart can be tricked for a moment. Keep good logs and good keys.
